newsitem.title: FRANCE: French opposition Socialists seek debate with Juppe.
newsitem.headline: French opposition Socialists seek debate with Juppe.

text.p: France's opposition Socialists challenged Prime Minister Alain Juppe on Saturday to agree to a face-to-face debate after he said he wanted the parliamentary election campaign to focus on issues rather than personal barbs.

"If Juppe honestly wants precise and detailed answers on the left's programme, he should accept an open and sincere face-to-face debate with (Socialist Party leader) Lionel Jospin," Socialist deputy Julien Dray said.
Juppe, leader of the Gaullist RPR party, said on Friday he hoped to steer the election campaign towards unemployment and other key voter concerns and away from mud-slinging.

"What I deeply desire is for the campaign to change tone," he told France 3 television. "Over the past two weeks it has largely consisted of personal attacks and partisan jibes. The time for such behaviour is over."
All sides in the two-round May 25-June 1 election have been sharpening their rhetoric as polls show the left within striking distance of pushing the governing centre-right out of power.
"Alain Juppe, who has been shooting from the hip from the start of the campaign, is sounding more and more like a poor lonesome cowboy," Dray said in a statement.
Policy arguments have broken out between the Socialists and the Communists, whose support the Socialists need to form a government should the left prevail.

Juppe, seen as deeply unpopular among voters in opinion polls, has agreed to a debate with Jospin only if they are joined by Communist Party leader Robert Hue and centrist Union for French Democracy (UDF) head Francois Leotard.
Jospin, on other hand, has insisted he should face Juppe alone.
The opposition has hammered away at Juppe, accusing him of giving the campaign an aggressive edge from the outset, when he declared it would be both "joyful and brutal".
The prime minister has also come under fire from his own allies over the centre-right's lacklustre strategy.

Gaullist President Jacques Chirac said this week his government had had to "wipe the slate clean" after years of Socialist misrule and urged voters to give him the "political stability indispensible for effective action".
Chirac sent shock waves through French politics when he decided last month to hold parliamentary elections nine months early despite a huge majority in the National Assembly.

A win for the centre-right would give it five more years of uninterrupted power, a possibility the left has attacked as a "blank cheque" for more government austerity in a drive to help France qualify for European monetary union.

The Socialists reject Chirac's attempt to blame them for France's record 12.8 percent unemployment, arguing the conservatives have been in power since 1993 and that it is now time to give the left a chance.
The centre-right says it is vital France stay the course to qualify for the single currency and succeed in an era of intensifying global economic competition.

Gaullist Jean-Francois Cope, who helped the RPR draft its economic platform, said one key reason Chirac had dissolved parliament early was to "break with the wait-and-see economic policies that are inevitable during the pre-election period".
Cope called on the next government to reform the civil service and state finances and to cut taxes and payroll charges.
The parliamentary elections were initially set for March 1998, at the same time Europe was due to determine which countries would be eligible for the initial shift to a single currency.
